question: What was one major provision introduced by the Pitt’s India Act of 1784 concerning the Court of Directors?
options: It granted them authority to make laws for Indian states
It allowed them to dissolve Indian provincial courts
It made them accountable to the British Government in civil/military affairs
It merged them with the Board of Control
explanation: The Pitt’s India Act, 1784, established a Board of Control to increase government regulation over the Company, to which the Court of Directors became accountable for civil, military, and revenue affairs. • This led to the introduction of a system of double government in India— trade remained with the Company, while political rights came under the control of the government.

subject: Polity
question: Fill in the blank: Pitt’s India Act 1784 created a six- member body called the ______ to supervise Company politics
explanation: To remove the defects of the Regulating Act of 1773, the British Parliament passed the Pitt’s India Act (1784). Under this, the commercial and political functions of the Company were separated. • A 6-member ‘Board of Control’ was established in London to manage and supervise the political affairs of the Company (such as military, civil, and revenue administration).

subject: Polity
question: The Governor General’s Council, as established by the Regulating Act, consisted of how many members?
explanation: • Under the Regulating Act of 1773, the Governor of Bengal was designated as the Governor-General of Bengal, and a four-member Executive Council (comprising Philip Francis, Clavering, Monson, and Barwell) was constituted. Decisions were made by a majority, and in the case of a tie, the Governor-General held a casting vote. Lord Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General under this Act. • Through this legislation, the Madras and Bombay Presidencies were made subordinate to Bengal. Later, the Pitt’s India Act (1784) reduced the number of council members from four to three.

subject: Polity
question: Under which Act was a Law Commission first established in India to codify and consolidate Indian laws?
explanation: • Under the Charter Act of 1833, the first Law Commission of India was established in 1834, chaired by Lord Macaulay. Its objective was to codify laws, including the Indian Penal Code, and to implement a uniform legal system throughout British India. • The first Law Commission of independent India was constituted in 1955, with M. C. Setalvad as its Chairman.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following pairs (Educational Event - Key Outcome/ Initiative) is correctly matched?
options: Charter Act, 1813 - Allocated funds for promotion of education
Macaulay’s Minute, 1835 - Emphasized traditional Sanskrit learning
Serampore Mission - Promoted technical education for elite Indians
Orientalist-Anglicist Debate - Resolved by Charter Act, 1833
explanation: Under the Charter Act of 1813, for the first time, the responsibility of the state for the spread of education in India was defined, and a provision was made to allocate an annual sum of 1 lakh rupees. • Under this same Act, Christian missionaries were permitted to come to India and propagate their religion, as well as to open schools and hospitals.

subject: Polity
question: Under Pitt’s India Act, what restriction was placed on the Governor General and Council?
options: They could not pass any civil law without Queen’s consent
They could not issue orders without majority support
They were forbidden to declare war or make treaties without approval
They had to resign after 5 years in office
explanation: The Pitt’s India Act 1784 prohibited the Governor-General and his Council from declaring war or entering into treaties without the permission of the Board of Control. This was the first attempt by the British Parliament to establish control over expansionist policies in India.

subject: Polity
question: What was the function of the Board of Control established by Pitt’s India Act?
options: To manage only military operations in India
To oversee taxation and local revenue
To control civil and military affairs in British India
To regulate trade between India and China
explanation: The Pitt’s India Act of 1784 introduced a system of dual government in which a 6-member Board of Control established full control over the political, civil, military, and revenue matters of the East India Company through the British Government. Meanwhile, the Court of Directors was restricted only to commercial matters.

subject: Polity
question: What change did the Regulating Act bring to the post of the Governor of Bengal?
options: He was required to report directly to the British Crown
He was reduced to a ceremonial position
His role was elevated to Governor- General with a council of four members
He was transferred to the Madras Presidency
explanation: • The Regulating Act of 1773 elevated the Governor of Bengal to the post of Governor-General of Bengal. Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General, who was assisted by a four-member executive council. • The Governors of Madras and Bombay were also made subordinate to the Governor-General of Bengal.

subject: Polity
question: The Regulating Act of 1773 primarily introduced changes in the Company’s administration in which two distinct areas?
options: Company’s Judicial system and revenue collection.
Company’s Military strategy and trade regulations.
Company’s constitution at home and territorial control in India.
Company’s relations with princely states and foreign policy.
explanation: • At the domestic level, the company’s constitution – mandatory reporting of revenue, military, and civil affairs to the British government, voting qualifications, tenure (1 year to 4 years), and election of the company’s Court of Directors was established. Through this, the management of the company in Britain was regulated. • Territorial Control in India – The Governor of Bengal was made the Governor-General (Warren Hastings was the first), along with a four- member Council. The foundation of centralized administration was laid by placing the Madras and Bombay Presidencies under Bengal. • Additionally, the Calcutta Supreme Court was established (judicial reform). Ans. (c) Rule of the British Crown

subject: Polity
question: Which administrative bodies were abolished after the enactment of the Government of India Act, 1858?
options: Board of Control and Court of Directors
Governor General’s Council and Privy Council
explanation: • The Government of India Act, 1858, terminated the rule of the East India Company and transferred the governance of India directly to the British Crown. Consequently, the Board of Control and the Court of Directors were abolished. In their place, the office of the Secretary of State for India and a 15-member Council of India were established. • Alongside these changes, the designation of the Governor-General was changed to Viceroy, and Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following statements is correct with reference to the Act passed by the British Parliament in 1858? I. The Governor-General of India was given the title of Viceroy. II. The British decided to respect the customary religious and social practices of the people in India.
explanation: • Under the Government of India Act of 1858, the Governor-General was given the title of Viceroy. • Along with this, the British government announced that they would respect the religious and social customs of the people of India. • Through this law, the governance of India passed from the ‘East India Company’ directly into the hands of the ‘British Crown’ (the Queen).

subject: Polity
question: The “Indian Councils Act of 1892” represented a limited expansion of Indian participation in the legislative councils.What was a notable feature of this Act regarding the selection of Indian members?
options: It introduced universal adult suffrage for the election of Indian members.
It allowed for the direct election of a majority of Indian members to the central legislative council.
It permitted the nomination of some Indian members by the Governor-General and provided for indirect election through electoral colleges.
It mandated equal representation for all religious communities in the legislative councils.
explanation: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 introduced a combination of indirect elections and nominations in the Legislative Councils, where Indian members were selected by the Governor- General on the recommendation of bodies such as district boards and universities. • This Act not only increased the number of non-official members but also expanded the democratic scope of the councils by granting them the right to discuss the budget and ask questions on matters of public interest.

subject: Polity
question: What was the role of the India Council established by the Government of India Act, 1858?
options: To advise the Secretary of State
To represent Indian opinion in Britain
explanation: Under the Government of India Act, 1858, a 15-member Council of India was constituted. It was an advisory body located in London, which assisted and advised the Secretary of State for India on administrative matters, and the Secretary of State himself was its chairman.

subject: Polity
question: The Government of India Act of 1935 primarily aimed to:
options: Establish a Dominion status for India
Provide for a federal structure with provincial autonomy
explanation: Explanation– The main objective of the Government of India Act 1935 was to establish an All India Federation, which would include the provinces of British India and the princely states. This Act abolished dyarchy in the provinces, granted them greater autonomy, and divided the powers between the Centre and the provinces through the Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent Lists. Furthermore, the Federal Court established in 1937 later laid the foundation for the Supreme Court of India, which ensured the independence of the judiciary.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following statements regarding the Government of India Act, 1919 is correctly matched with its constitutional implication?
options: Transferred and Reserved subjects – Created functional overlap between central and provincial powers
Creation of bicameralism – Introduced two houses at the central level for the first time
Establishment of Public Service Commission – Gave financial control to Indian members in the Viceroy’s Council
Introduction of diarchy in provinces – Empowered Indian ministers to control defence and foreign affairs
explanation: A bicameral legislature was established at the Centre by the Act of 1919. It consisted of two houses: 1. Council of State 2. Central Legislative Assembly. • Under the Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms), provincial subjects were divided into two parts along with diarchy in the provinces— Reserved (with the Governor) and Transferred (with the Indian Ministers).

subject: Polity
question: Fill in the blank: The Government of India Act 1919 created a bicameral central legislature with the Council of State and the ___.
explanation: • The Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) es tablished a bicameral legislature at the Centre for the first time. • The Upper House being the Council of State and the Lower House being the Central Legislative Assembly. • This Act introduced dyarchy in the provinces and extended communal representation to Sikhs, Christians, and Anglo-Indians.

subject: Polity
question: Fill in the blank: The Federal Court of India, as provided under the Government of India Act, 1935, was established in the year _____.
explanation: • Under the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, a Federal Court was established. • This court became functional on 1 October, 1937, and later in 1950, the Supreme Court of India was established in its place.

subject: Polity
question: Which major constitutional feature was first introduced by the Government of India Act, 1935 and later adopted in the Indian Constitution?
explanation: • Under the Government of India Act, 1935, ‘Dyarchy’ was abolished in the provinces and ‘Provincial Autonomy’ was introduced. • Along with this, there was a proposal to establish an ‘All India Federation’, in which a clear division of powers was made between the Centre and the units (Provinces and Princely States). • In the series of constitutional reforms in India, the British Parliament passed the Government of India Act, 1935, following the failures of the Government of India Act, 1919.

subject: Polity
question: Who hand-calligraphed the original manuscript of the Indian Constitution?
explanation: The original manuscript of the Indian Constitution was handwritten by Prem Behari Narain Raizada in a beautiful calligraphic style in English. Each page was decorated by the artist Nandlal Bose and his disciples.

subject: Polity
question: Who is regarded as the chief architect of the Indian Constitution?
explanation: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is called the architect and father of the Indian Constitution. He was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, and based on the study of the constitutions of various countries, he played a decisive role in the framing of the Constitution suited to Indian conditions.

subject: Polity
question: Who was the constitutional advisor to the Constituent assembly of India?
explanation: B. N. Rau was appointed as the Constitutional Advisor to the Constituent Assembly in 1946 and he prepared the initial draft of the Indian Constitution, which was later worked upon by the Drafting Committee headed by Dr. Ambedkar.

question: Who was the Chairman of the “Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities, and Tribal and Excluded Areas” in the Constituent Assembly?

explanation: The Credentials Committee of the Constituent Assembly was chaired by Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar. question: Which of the following is correctly matched with their leadership role in the Constituent Assembly (During the making of the Indian constitution)?

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar - Head of the Committee on the Functions of the Assembly
N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar - Chairman of the Order of Business Committee
K.M. Munshi - Leader of the Committee on Fundamental Rights
explanation: G.V. Mavalankar was the Chairman of the Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly. He also became the Speaker of the first Lok Sabha of India. Other Committees: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar: Chairman of the Drafting Committee. K.M. Munshi: Chairman of the Order of Business Committee. Sardar Patel: Chairman of the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities.

subject: Polity
question: Who was the chairman of the drafting committee of the constituent assembly?
explanation: The Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, was constituted on August 29, 1947, to prepare the draft of the Constitution. The committee consisted of a total of seven members, including the Chairman.

subject: Polity
question: In which year did the Indian Constitution come into effect?
explanation: The Indian Constitution was adopted on November 26, 1949, but it was fully implemented on January 26, 1950. On this day, India became a Republic and Dr. Rajendra Prasad took charge as the first President. To commemorate this day, Republic Day is celebrated every year in India on January 26.

question: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from USSR (Now Russia)?
options: Residuary powers vest with the centre
Centre appoints the Governors at the states
explanation: Currently, under Article 51A, there are 11 Fundamental Duties. These Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution through the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, based on the recommendations of the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee. These provisions are inspired by the Constitution of the former Soviet Union (USSR).

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from Canada?
options: Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme court
explanation: Under Article 143 of the Indian Constitution, the President may seek the advice of the Supreme Court on any question of law or fact; this “advisory jurisdiction” has been borrowed from Canada. In addition, the federal system with a strong centre and the process of appointment of Governors were also taken from the Canadian Constitution.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from United States of America?
options: Centrifugal form of federalism where the centre is stronger than the states.
explanation: In the Indian Constitution, the provisions for Fundamental Rights, Judicial Review, and the process of Impeachment of the President have been borrowed from the Constitution of the United States of America. The Concurrent List has been taken from Australia and Single Citizenship has been taken from the British Constitution.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from Japan?
options: Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme court
explanation: The “procedure established by law” mentioned in Article 21 of the Indian Constitution is inspired by the Japanese Constitution. It means that the State can deprive a person of their life or personal liberty only through the procedure prescribed by law.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from Australia?
options: Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme court
Removal of Supreme Court and High court judges
explanation: In the Indian Constitution, the provisions for the Concurrent List, freedom of trade and commerce, and the joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament have been taken from the Constitution of Australia. • The procedure for amendment of the Constitution (Article 368) has been adopted from South Africa, and the procedure for the removal of judges has been taken from America.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution is NOT borrowed from Australia?
options: Joint sitting of the two houses
Election of members of the Rajya Sabha
explanation: In the Indian Constitution, the procedure for the ‘election of members of Rajya Sabha’ has been taken from the Constitution of South Africa, and not from Australia. Whereas, the provisions for the Concurrent List, joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament, and freedom of trade and commerce have been adopted from the Constitution of Australia.

subject: Polity
question: Which constitutional features in India are linked to the Australian Constitution?
explanation: Provisions borrowed for the Ordinance from the Australian Constitution: • In the Indian Constitution, the provisions of the Concurrent List, the freedom of trade and commerce (Articles 301–307), and the joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament (Article 108) have been taken from the Australian Constitution.

subject: Polity
question: The Indian Constitution is often described as ‘quasi-federal’ or ‘federal in form, unitary in spirit’ primarily due to which characteristic?
options: The equal representation of states in the Rajya Sabha.
The presence of a written constitution.
Strong centralizing tendencies and powers of the Union Government.
The existence of an independent judiciary.
explanation: The Indian Constitution was described as ‘Quasi-federal’ by the famous jurist K. C. Wheare. It is called ‘Quasi-federal’ because it has a federal system (division of powers between the Centre and the States), a written Constitution, and an independent judiciary, but at the same time, the extensive powers given to the Centre and emergency provisions make it unitary in practice. Therefore, it is described as “federal in form but unitary in spirit.”

subject: Polity
question: Identify the following constitutional attributes with their respective democratic values:
options: a – ii, b – i, c – iv, d – iii
a – i, b – ii, c – iii, d – iv
a – iii, b – iv, c – i, d – ii
a – iv, b – iii, c – ii, d – i
explanation: Fundamental Duties (iii): These express the responsibilities of citizens and their commitment towards the nation. • Equal Suffrage (iv): It is based on the principle of universal adult franchise, where every adult citizen has the right to cast an equal vote. • Local Self-Government (i): Under the 73rd and 74th Amendments, Panchayats and Municipalities strengthen democracy at the grassroots level. • Religious Freedom (ii): It ensures respect for the individual conscience of citizens and guarantees the freedom to follow and practise the religion of their choice.

subject: Polity
question: Which of these is not a feature of Indian federalism?
explanation: The nature of the Indian Constitution is ‘quasi-federal’, which includes both federal and unitary features. Unlike the USA, there is no provision for ‘dual citizenship’ in India; only ‘single citizenship’ has been provided for in India.

subject: Polity
question: What is the supreme law of India?)
explanation: In India, the Constitution is supreme. While the Parliament has the power to make laws and the Supreme Court to interpret them, both function within the framework of the Constitution. The Preamble’s phrase “We, the People of India” clarifies that sovereignty and ultimate legal power reside in the people and this sacred document.

subject: Polity
question: The division of powers between the Union (Central) Government and State Governments in India is a key feature of its constitutional structure. What term describes this system?
explanation: The division of powers between the Central and State governments in India is known as the Federal System. • Under this arrangement, the Constitution clearly defines the subjects on which the Centre or the States can legislate. • However, the Indian system is also described as ‘Quasi-federal’ because the Central Government becomes more powerful during situations like an Emergency.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following statements about federalism in India is true?
options: States have the right to secede from the Union
There is rigid division of powers
explanation: The most prominent feature of Indian Federalism is that states do not have the right to secede from the Union. According to Dr. Ambedkar, the Indian Union is not the result of an ‘agreement’ between states, but is an indestructible framework. • India is called an “indestructible Union of destructible states” because the Central Government can change the boundaries or names of states, but no state has the power to become independent from India.

subject: Polity
question: Consider the following statements: 1. Indian federalism is biased towards the Centre 2. The Constitution uses the word ‘federal’ explicitly Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation: In the Indian Constitution, more powers are given to the Centre (such as Article 356 and residuary powers); therefore, it is tilted towards the Centre. Hence, Statement 1 is correct. • The word ‘Federal’ is not mentioned anywhere in the Constitution; in Article 1, India is described as a ‘Union of States’. Therefore, Statement 2 is incorrect.

subject: Polity
question: The Preamble to the Indian Constitution declares India to be a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. Which of these terms were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976?
explanation: Three words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976— “Socialist”, “Secular” and “Integrity”. Due to the extensive reforms in this amendment, it is also called the ‘Mini Constitution’.

subject: Polity
question: How does the Preamble of the Constitution describe India?
explanation: The Preamble of the Constitution describes India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, and Democratic Republic. • In 1976, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act amended the Preamble for the first time to include the words Socialist, Secular, and Integrity. Therefore, it is clear that these terms were not part of the original Preamble of the Indian Constitution.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following words is mentioned in the preamble of the Indian constitution regarding ‘Justice’?
explanation: • In the Preamble of the Indian Constitution, it is mentioned to ensure three forms of ‘justice’: social, economic and political justice. • Secular, Socialist, and Sovereign are terms related to the nature of the state, not to ‘justice’.

subject: Polity
question: Which Article empowers Parliament to alter state boundaries and form new states?
explanation: Article 3 empowers the Parliament to form new states, change boundaries, increase or decrease areas, and alter names. This is done through an ordinary bill and the opinion of the State Legislature is sought, which is not binding. • Article 1: List of States/Union Territories of India and the structure of the Union. • Article 2: Related to the admission of new states into the Union. • Article 4: Consequential/incidental provisions for laws made under Articles 2 and 3.

subject: Polity
question: Which Article defines State and Union Territories for the purposes of the Constitution?
explanation: • This provision is in Article 1 of the Indian Constitution, which states that “Bharat, that is India, shall be a Union of States” and the states and their territories are mentioned in the First Schedule. • Article 3 is related to the formation of new states, while Articles 239 and 240 are related to the administration and regulations of Union Territories (UTs).

subject: Polity
question: Whose death led to creation of the first linguistic state of India, Andhra Pradesh?
explanation: The widespread public outcry following the 56-day fast unto death and subsequent demise (December 15, 1952) of the Gandhian freedom fighter Potti Sriramulu forced the government to form Andhra Pradesh on a linguistic basis from Madras State. As a result, on October 1, 1953, India’s first linguistic state for Telugu-speaking people came into existence.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following article of the Indian Constitution is related with Admission or establishment of new States?
explanation: Article 2 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Parliament to admit into the Union or establish ‘new states’ by law. This relates to those states which were not previously part of the Indian Union (for example, the admission of Sikkim in 1975).

subject: Polity
question: An Indian state can be divided or its boundary altered by which of the following?
explanation: Under Article 3 of the Indian Constitution, the Parliament has the power to: • Divide any state, • Alter its boundaries, • Or form a new state. In this process, only the opinion of the concerned State Legislature is sought, which is not binding.

subject: Polity
question: Read the following statements and mark the correct option: Assertion (A): Potti Sriramulu fasted unto death for the formation of Andhra Pradesh Reason (R): His death marked the beginning of linguistic state formation in India
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: Potti Sriramulu undertook a fast unto death for 56 days in 1952, during which he died; as a result, Andhra State was formed in 1953 and later, the process of reorganisation of states (1956) on a linguistic basis began.

subject: Polity
question: The integration of the princely states into the Indian Union after 1947 involved a complex interplay of political negotiation, popular movements, and, at times, coercion. Which of the following factors most significantly undermined the initial aspirations of some princely rulers to maintain independent or autonomous status?
options: The overwhelming military superiority of the newly formed Pakistani state, compelling the rulers to seek protection within India.
The consistent and unwavering support provided by the British government to the princely states seeking independence.
The strong undercurrent of popular will within the princely states favoring accession to India, often expressed through organized movements and protests.
The economic prosperity and stability offered by remaining independent, making integration into the financially strained Indian Union D. unattractive.
explanation: • In 1947, the rulers of the princely states desired to remain independent; however, the people initiated massive popular movements for integration into India through organizations like the ‘Praja Mandal’. • Sardar Patel utilized this public pressure and diplomacy to compel the rulers to sign the ‘Instrument of Accession’.

subject: Polity
question: Fill in the blanks: Zonal Councils were created by the _______ Act, 1956.
explanation: • The Zonal Councils were established under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. • The recommendations of the States Reorganisation Commission were based on the Fazal Ali Commission, 1953. • Following this, India was divided into 14 states and 6 union territories, and the A, B, C, D categories were abolished. • In the year 1953, Andhra Pradesh became the first state to be formed on a linguistic basis.

subject: Polity
question: Arrange the following events in chronological order: a. Eastern Zonal Council meeting 2022 b. States Reorganisation Act passed c. First Central Zonal Council meeting
explanation: • After independence, the reorganization of Indian states was primarily done on a linguistic basis to ensure administrative efficiency, cultural identity, and political stability • Under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, five Zonal Councils (Northern, Southern, Eastern, Western, and Central) were established, which serve as a platform for Centre-State and inter- state coordination. • This Act was passed in 1956; following this, the first meeting of the Central Zonal Council was held in 1957, and the 25th meeting of the Eastern Zonal Council was organized in Kolkata in December 2022.

subject: Polity
question: Under which article of the Indian Constitution is the Right to Equality guaranteed?
explanation: The Right to Equality is ensured under Articles 14 to 18 in the Indian Constitution. Article 14 relates to ‘Equality before the law’; Article 15 prohibits ‘discrimination on the basis of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth’; • Article 16 ‘provides equal opportunities to all citizens in public employment’; • Article 17 prohibits untouchability to ensure social justice; and Article 18 relates to the abolition of all titles except military/academic ones.

subject: Polity
question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws?
explanation: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees that no person within the territory of India shall be denied ‘equality before the law’ and ‘equal protection of the laws’. This right applies to both citizens and foreigners (except enemy aliens).

subject: Polity
question: Which article of the Constitution abolishes ‘Untouchability’?
explanation: • Article 17 of the Indian Constitution abolishes ‘Untouchability’ and forbids its practice in any form. • It is a Fundamental Right mentioned in Part III of the Constitution, falling under the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18).

subject: Polity
question: The concept of “Reasonable Classifi cation” as a limitation to the Right to Equality (Article 14) was established in which case?

State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Golaknath Case v. State of Punjab & Anrs.

question: Which of the following writ is issued by a higher court (High Court or Supreme Court) when a lower court has considered a case going beyond its jurisdiction?
explanation: When any lower court or judicial authority begins to hear a case by going beyond its jurisdiction, an order of prohibition is issued by the High Court or the Supreme Court. options: Article 32; it is called the “heart and soul” of the Constitution
Article 226; it is a protective mechanism for Directive Principles
Article 21; it deals with personal liberty only
Article 14; it ensures equality before law
explanation: Article – 32: It provides the Right to Constitutional Remedies and is linked to Fundamental Rights because a petition can be filed directly in the Supreme Court in case of their violation. Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar called it the “heart and soul” of the Constitution. Under this, the Supreme Court can issue five types of writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-Warranto). Ans. (a) Others

subject: Polity
question: Which part of the Indian Constitution is known as the “Magna Carta of India” and guarantees fundamental rights to the citizens?
explanation: Part III of the Indian Constitution (Fundamental Rights) is called the “Magna Carta of India” because it provides a constitutional guarantee of fundamental rights to the citizens. These rights are enforceable by the courts, which means that in case of their violation, a petition can be filed under Article 32 and 226.

subject: Polity
question: Arrange the following Fundamental Rights in the order they are listed in the Indian Constitution: 1. Right to Constitutional Remedies 2. Right to Freedom 3. Right against Exploitation 4. Right to Equality
explanation: S.No. Fundamental Rights Articles 1. Right to Equality 14–18 2. Right to Freedom 19–22 3. Right against Exploitation 23–24 4. Right to Freedom of Religion 25–28 5. Cultural & Educational Rights 29–30 6. Right to Constitutional Remedies

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following Fundamental Rights are not available to foreigners in India? 1. Right against discrimination (Article 15) 2. Freedom of speech and expression (Article 19(1)(a)) 3. Right to protection in respect of conviction (Article 20) 4. Right to life and personal liberty (Article 21)
explanation: Under the Indian Constitution, Article 15 (Right against Discrimination) and Article 19 (Freedom of Speech and Expression) are specifically reserved for Indian citizens only and are not available to foreigners. • In contrast, Article 20 (Protection in respect of conviction for offences) and Article 21 (Right to Life) are considered fundamental human rights, which are provided equally to both citizens and foreigners. • Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 of the Indian Constitution are the only rights strictly limited to citizens.

subject: Polity
question: Fill in the Blank: Doctrine of Severability allows the ______.part of a law to be retained .
explanation: Under Article 13, validity is provided to the Doctrine of Severability, which declares laws that violate Fundamental Rights as void. • The Doctrine of Severability states that if a part of a law is unconstitutional, then only that specific offending part will be removed, and not the entire law.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights?
explanation: The Right to Property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978. By removing it from Fundamental Rights, the Right to Property has been made a legal right under Article 300A.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following is true about Fundamental Rights and DPSPs?
options: Both are justiciable and enforceable by courts
DPSPs override Fundamental Rights when in conflict
Fundamental Rights are justiciable, but DPSPs are not
DPSPs are guaranteed by the Constitution; Fundamental Rights are optional
explanation: Fundamental Rights (Part III) are justiciable and a person can go to court in case of their violation, whereas Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are non-justiciable policy guidelines • In case of a conflict, Fundamental Rights generally prevail over DPSP. In case of violation of Fundamental Rights, the Supreme Court under Article 32 or the High Court under Article 226 can enforce them by issuing writs.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following statement is correct regarding the fundamental rights given in the Indian constitution? I. Article 30 is related with Abolition of titles. II. Article 22 is related with Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc.
explanation: Abolition of titles falls under Article 18, whereas Article 30 grants minorities the right to establish educational institutions. • Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc., comes under Article 24, whereas Article 22 provides protection against arrest and detention in certain cases.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following best reflects the constitutional dilemma in implementing the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in India, as discussed in debates surrounding Article 44 and Article 25?
options: UCC allows gender-based personal law systems to remain untouched under Article 14
UCC enforces cooperative federalism by giving states legislative powers on personal law
UCC operationalises the secular ethos by completely eliminating all religious laws
UCC aligns with Article 44 but may be seen to infringe upon religious freedom under Article 25
explanation: Article 44 directs the State to implement a Uniform Civil Code, while Article 25 provides freedom of religion to citizens. For this reason, a constitutional dilemma arises between secularism and religious freedom in the implementation of the UCC. Aspect Article 44 (UCC) Article 25 (Freedom of Religion) Nature Directive Mandatory/ Fundamental Objective National unity and gender justice Protection of religious identity Approach Secular Law Personal belief

subject: Polity
question: The concept of “Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)” in the Indian Constitution has been borrowed from the Constitution of which country?
explanation: • In the Indian Constitution, the concept of Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) has been taken from the Irish Constitution. • It is a noteworthy fact that Ireland itself had taken this concept from the Spanish Constitution.

subject: Polity
question: What does the Uniform Civil Code primarily aim to achieve?
explanation: • According to the Directive Principles of State Policy mentioned in Article 44 of the Constitution, there should be a uniform law for personal matters for all citizens of the country, regardless of their religion, gender, or caste. • Uttarakhand is the first state of independent India to implement the Uniform Civil Code.

subject: Polity
question: Which section of the Indian constitution ensure social and economic reforms in a country?
explanation: The Directive Principles of State Policy, described in Part IV (Articles 36- 51) of the Constitution, provide directions to the State that help in establishing social and economic democracy in the country. • These principles are not enforceable by the courts, but are considered fundamental in the governance of the country.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following statement is correct regarding the directive principles of state policy given in the Indian constitution? I. They are not enforceable by any court. II. It shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
explanation: Article 37 clarifies that the Directive Principles cannot be legally enforced by the courts (non-justiciable), but they are ‘fundamental’ in the governance of the country. • Therefore, it is the moral and constitutional duty of the government to keep these principles (such as equal pay for equal work, Gram Panchayat, etc.) in mind while making policies and laws.

subject: Polity
question: Article 51 of the Indian constitution is related with which of the following?
options: Promotion of international peace and security
Organization of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry
explanation: Article 51 of the Indian Constitution falls under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). • It directs the State to: promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage the settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following article of the Indian constitution promotes equal justice and free legal aid?
explanation: The provision for equal justice and free legal aid in the Indian Constitution is contained in Article 39A. This provision was added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976). • According to Article 39A, it is the duty of the State to ensure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.

subject: Polity
question: What is the primary objective of a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in India?
options: To establish a common criminal law for all citizens
To unify direct and indirect tax laws
To provide a common set of personal laws for all citizens, irrespective of religion
To standardize administrative procedures across all states
explanation: The objective of the Uniform Civil Code (Article 44) is to establish a uniform set of personal laws (marriage, divorce, inheritance, property, and adoption) for all citizens, regardless of their religion, based on the principle of ‘One Nation, One Rule’. • Uttarakhand is the first state to implement the UCC after independence, while in Goa, the ‘Common Civil Code’ has already been in force since the Portuguese rule.

subject: Polity
question: What makes the Goa Civil Code distinct from other personal laws in India?
options: It is a uniform civil code for all communities regardless of religion.
It is based on British common law
explanation: • The Goa Civil Code is a unique example in India, as it applies equally to all citizens regardless of religion, caste, or community. • It is not entirely based on British Common Law, but rather has its roots in the Portuguese Civil Code, 1867.

subject: Polity
question: The concept of Uniform Civil Code is a part of which category of principles in the Indian Constitution?
explanation: • The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) is mentioned in Article 44 of the Indian Constitution, which comes under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). • Article 51A of the Indian Constitution mentions the Fundamental Duties of citizens. • Fundamental Rights are described in Part III (Article 12-35) of the Indian Constitution.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following is a Fundamental Duty mentioned in the Indian Constitution?
options: To vote in the Lok Sabha election
To educate child up to 18 years of age
explanation: According to Article 51A (g) of the Constitution, it is the Fundamental Duty of every Indian citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following is a Fundamental Duty mentioned in the Indian Constitution?
options: To respect one’s parents and teachers
To take part in village panchayat
explanation: According to Article 51A (i) of the Constitution, “to safeguard public property and to abjure violence” is the fundamental duty of every Indian citizen. These duties were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committe.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following is a Fundamental Duty mentioned in the Indian Constitution?
options: To value the rich heritage of our composite culture
To not indulge in corrupt practices
To respect freedom of speech of others
explanation: Under Article 51A(f) of the Constitution, ‘to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture’ is a Fundamental Duty. Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty mentioned in the Indian Constitution?
options: To respect ideals of the constitution
explanation: In the Indian Constitution, Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles of State Policy are two different concepts. • It is the responsibility of the State to ensure the separation of the executive and the judiciary, whereas it is the duty of the citizens to respect the national flag and the Constitution. • The separation of the judiciary from the executive is a part of the ‘Directive Principles of State Policy’ (DPSP) under Article 50. Fundamental Duties are mentioned in Article 51A, which include respecting the national flag and the national anthem.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty mentioned in the Indian Constitution?
options: To value the rich heritage of our composite culture
explanation: The Fundamental Duties of citizens are given in Article 51A of the Indian Constitution. These include the protection of national unity, the development of a scientific temper, and respect for cultural heritage. • Promoting cooperative societies is not a Fundamental Duty. This subject is related to the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) and was added by the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011.

subject: Polity
question: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the extent of executive power of the Union?
explanation: Article 73 of the Indian Consti- tution provides that the executive power of the Union shall extend to all matters on which Parliament has the power to make laws. It is also limited to the exercise of the rights conferred by any treaty or agreement. • Article 52 declares that “There shall be a President of India.” • Article 75 deals with other provisions related to the Prime Minister, such as appointment, tenure, responsibilities and oath.

subject: Polity
question: Solicitor General of India is appointed by the President of India. 2. A candidate contesting for the post of the President of India is required to make a security deposit of `15,000. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
explanation: The Solicitor General of India is appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet. It is the second-highest law officer after the Attorney General and is a statutory (not constitutional) post; therefore, statement 1 is incorrect. • A presidential candidate is required to deposit a security amount of `15,000 in the Reserve Bank of India (RBI); thus, statement 2 is correct.

subject: Polity
question: The Governor can dissolve the State Legislative Assembly. 2. The President has no such power regarding the Lok Sabha. Which of the above is/are correct?
explanation: Under Article 174(2)(b), the Governor can dissolve the Legislative Assembly on the advice of the Council of Ministers and also at his own discretion in special circumstances; therefore, statement 1 is correct. • Under Article 85(2)(b), the President has the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha, which he generally exercises on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister; therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

subject: Polity
question: Parliament can create All India Services with approval of Rajya Sabha. 2. Article 312 mentions ‘Security Services’ as part of All India Services. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
explanation: Under Article 312, if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two- thirds majority, Parliament can create a new All India Service; therefore, statement 1 is correct. • Article 312 does not mention ‘security services’ but only mentions administrative and police services, therefore statement 2 is incorrect.

subject: Polity
question: The President can dissolve Lok Sabha on his own discretion. 2. The Governor appoints the Chief Minister in a hung assembly. 3. The Governor has no role in Money Bills. Which of the above is/are correct?
explanation: The President cannot dissolve the Lok Sabha at their own discretion, but only on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect. • In the event of a Hung Assembly (lack of a clear majority), the Governor exercises their discretionary power to appoint the Chief Minister. Therefore, statement 2 is correct. • In a State, a Money Bill is introduced only with the prior permission (recommendation) of the Governor, making their role mandatory. Therefore, statement 3 is also incorrect.

subject: Polity
question: Delegated legislation is made by administrative authorities. 2. It cannot be challenged in a court of law. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
explanation: This is the law made by administrative officers (the executive) using the power of Parliament; therefore, statement 1 is correct. • Delegated legislation can be challenged in court (if it is against the Constitution or the parent Act); therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

subject: Polity
question: Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill. 2. Every Financial Bill is a Money Bill. 3. Which of the above statements is/ are correct?
explanation: All Money Bills are Financial Bills because they deal with specific matters mentioned in Article 110; hence, Statement 1 is correct. • All Financial Bills are not Money Bills; only those bills are called Money Bills which contain provisions exclusively related to Article 110. Therefore, Statement 2 is incorrect. • The final decision on whether a bill is a Money Bill or not lies with the Speaker of the Lok Sabha/Speaker of the Legislative Assembly.

subject: Polity
question: Which body is responsible for resolving disputes related to the election of the President of India?
explanation: According to Article 71 of the In dian Constitution, if any doubt or dis pute arises regarding the election of the President, the Supreme Court of India has the sole and exclusive authority to inquire and decide upon it. • This provision ensures the fairness, transparency, and constitutional validity of the Presidential election.

subject: Polity
question: Only the PM can recommend President’s Rule under Article 356 of the Constitution. Which of the statements is/are correct ?
explanation: Under Article 85, the Prime Minister can advise the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, and under Article 174, the Chief Minister can advise the dissolution of the Legislative Assembly. Therefore, statement 1 is correct. • Under Article 356, the recommendation for President’s Rule is made by the Governor, not by the Prime Minister; therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

subject: Polity
question: The Vice-President of India is part of which branch of the government?
explanation: The Vice-President of India is a part of both the executive and legislative branches of the government. According to the Constitution, the Vice-President is a part of the executive and is the second- highest executive official of the country after the President. His main objective is to ensure continuity in case the office of the President suddenly becomes vacant (Article 65). • On the other hand, his practical role is primarily ‘legislative’, because as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, he controls the dignity and procedures of the legislative house, while under Article 64, he also conducts legislative functions as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

subject: Polity
question: Who succeeded M. Venkaiah Naidu as the Vice President of India in 2022?
explanation: Jagdeep Dhankhar took the oath as the 14th Vice President of India on August 11, 2022. He succeeded M. Venkaiah Naidu, whose term ended on August 10, 2022.

subject: Polity
question: Who holds the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha prior to the completion of its tenure?
explanation: The constitutional power to dissolve the Lok Sabha before the completion of its five-year term rests with the President of India, who acts on the advice of the Prime Minister under Article 85(2)(b).

subject: Polity
question: If someone becomes a minister or the Prime Minister without being a Member of Parliament, they must get elected to the Parliament within months or they will have to vacate the office.
explanation: According to Article 75(5) of the Indian Constitution, if a person is appointed as a Minister or Prime Minister without being a member of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha), they must be elected to either House of Parliament within six months from the date of their appointment. • If they fail to become a member during this period, they must resign from their post.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following veto powers is not available to the President of India?
explanation: The veto powers of the Indian President are slightly different compared to those of the American President. In India, Article 111 gives the President the power to take decisions on bills passed by the Parliament. • Absolute veto, suspensive veto, and pocket veto are available to the President of India. Qualified veto is not available to the President in India.

subject: Polity
question: What is the minimum age required to contest the Presidential election in India?
explanation: Under Article 58 of the Constitution, the qualifications for the office of the President have been prescribed. According to this, it is mandatory for a candidate to be a citizen of India and to have completed the minimum age of 35 years. • Under Part V (The Union) of the Constitution, Articles 52 to 62 relate to the office, election, qualifications, and impeachment of the President. Ans. (a) 9. Consider the following statements: 1. Both the Prime Minister (PM) and Chief Minister (CM) can advise dissolution of the respective Lower House.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following statements regarding the constitutional responsibility of the Council of Ministers (CoM) is/are correct? 1. The Union Council of Ministers is collectively accountable to the Lok Sabha. 2. In states with bicameral legislatures, the State CoM is collectively responsible to the Legislative Council.
explanation: According to Article 75(3), the Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha; hence, Statement 1 is correct. According to Article 164(2), the State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly, and not to the Legislative Council (even if the state has a bicameral legislature). Therefore, Statement 2 is incorrect.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following statements regarding the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and State legislatures is correct?
options: The State legislature can legislate on matters enumerated in the Union List
The Union legislature can legislate on matters in the Concurrent List only with State approval
The Union Government can issue directions to the States under Article 256
The Union and States have equal powers on matters in the Union List
explanation: Under Article 256, the Central Government can give directions to the states to ensure compliance with the Constitution and the laws of the Centre. The distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States is provided in Part XI (Articles 245–255) of the Indian Constitution. Ans. (c) 12. Read the below statements:

subject: Polity
question: The President is elected by an electoral college, while the Governor is_____.
explanation: According to Article 155 of the Constitution, the Governor of a State is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. The Governor does not have a fixed tenure; he holds office during the pleasure of the President (Article 156).

subject: Polity
question: Who is the 15th President of India?
explanation: Droupadi Murmu took the oath as the 15th President of India on July 25, 2022. She is the first tribal woman to hold this supreme constitutional office and the second woman President after Pratibha Patil. Along with this, she is also the first President to be born in independent India. Ans. (c) 15. Consider the following statements:

subject: Polity
question: How many members can the President of India nominate to the Rajya Sabha?
explanation: Under Article 80 of the Constitution, the President has the power to nominate 12 members to the Rajya Sabha. These members are eminent persons who possess special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as literature, science, art and social service.

subject: Polity
question: Who is the 16th Attorney General of India?
explanation: R. Venkataramani is the 16th Attorney General of India, who was appointed to this post in the year 2022. He succeeded K. K. Venugopal (15th Attorney General). • The Attorney General (Mahanyayavadi) is the highest law officer of India, who is appointed by the President under Article 76 of the Constitution.

subject: Polity
question: Who among the following holds office during the pleasure of the President of India?
options: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
explanation: In India, the Attorney General of India is the official who holds office during the pleasure of the President. According to Article 76 of the Constitution, the Attorney General is appointed by the President and remains in office at the will of the President. • In contrast, positions such as the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, the Chief Justice, and the Chief Election Commissioner have a fixed tenure and enjoy constitutional security of tenure.

subject: Polity
question: Which constitutional authority decides on the disqualification of a Member of State Legislature under the Anti- Defection Law?
explanation: Under the 10th Schedule of the Indian Constitution (Anti-Defection Law), the decision regarding the disqualification of a member of a State Legislature is taken by the Speaker or the Chairman of the House. However, in the Kihoto Hollohan (1992) case, the Supreme Court clarified that this decision of the Speaker is not final and is subject to Judicial Review. Ans. (b) Parliament (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha)

subject: Polity
question: The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha (House of the People) as stipulated by the Constitution is:
explanation: Article 81 of the Constitution is related to the composition of the Lok Sabha. According to the Indian Constitution, the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha has been fixed at 552, out of which 530 members are from the States, 20 members are from the Union Territories, and 2 members were nominated from the Anglo-Indian community (abolished by the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019).

subject: Polity
question: What is the total number of houses that make up the Indian Parliament?
explanation: According to Article 79, the Parliament consists of the President and two houses: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. While the Lok Sabha represents the people and has a term of 5 years, the Rajya Sabha acts as the Council of States and is a permanent house that cannot be dissolved. Ans. (b) 22. Consider the following statements:

subject: Polity
question: How many members are nominated by the President of India for the Rajya Sabha?
explanation: Under Article 80 of the Indian Constitution, the President of India nominates a total of 12 members to the Rajya Sabha. These members are persons who possess special knowledge or practical experience in the fields of literature, science, art, and social service.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following scenarios could validly lead to the impeachment of the President of India?
options: Refusing to dissolve Lok Sabha on the advice of the Cabinet
Declining to sign a bill passed by Parliament
Willfully acting against a constitutional provision.
Failing to address the nation on Independence Day
explanation: According to Article 61 of the Indian Constitution, impeachment proceedings against the President can only be initiated on the ground of “violation of the Constitution.” If the President willfully acts against the provisions of the Constitution, it constitutes a valid ground for impeachment. Ans. (c) 25. Consider the following statements:

subject: Polity
question: Fill in the blanks: The Rajya Sabha’s special power under Art 249 allows it to authorise Parliament to legislate on a ___ List subject
explanation: Under Article 249, if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting that it is necessary in the national interest, then Parliament acquires the power to make laws on subjects in the State List. • This power is temporary and remains effective only for the duration of the resolution.

subject: Polity
question: Consider the statements about the Rajya Sabha: 1) Rajya Sabha is a continuing house of the Parliament, immune to dissolution under any circumstance. 2) Rajya Sabha members serve staggered six-year terms, with one- third retiring every two years.
explanation: Rajya Sabha is a permanent house, which is not subject to dissolution, and one-third of its members retire every two years. This house reflects the federal nature and protects the interests of the states. • Its maximum strength is 250, of which 238 are elected and 12 are nominated by the President. Ans. (c) 28. Consider the following statements:

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following statement is correct regarding the election of Vice president of India? I. He should have completed 35 years of age. II. He should be qualified for election as a member of the Council of States.
explanation: The election and qualifications of the Vice-President are described in Article 66(3) of the Indian Constitution. Since the Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, their qualifications have a direct relationship with the Rajya Sabha. • A minimum age of 35 years is mandatory for the office of Vice- President, and the candidate must possess the qualifications to become a member of the Rajya Sabha.

subject: Polity
question: For how many years does the President of India hold office?
explanation: According to Article 56 of the Indian Constitution, the term of the President is 5 years. The President is elected by the Electoral College mentioned in Article 54, which includes the elected members of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of the States. The minimum age to become President is 35 years and the person must possess the qualifications to become a member of the Lok Sabha. • The oath of office to the President is administered by the Chief Justice of India (CJI); in their absence, the senior-most judge administers the oath.

subject: Polity
question: Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with sessions of Parliament?
explanation: Article 85 of the Indian Constitution is related to the sessions of Parliament. • Under this, the President has the power to summon sessions of Parliament, prorogue sessions, and dissolve the Lok Sabha.

subject: Polity
question: The Vice President of India can be removed from office by______.
options: Resolution passed by the Council of States and agreed to by the House of the People
Resolution passed by both Houses of Parliament with one-third majority
The President on the advice of the Prime Minister
explanation: According to Article 67(b) of the Constitution of India, the process for removing the Vice-President from office is as follows- • A resolution must be passed by the Rajya Sabha, and the agreement of the Lok Sabha must be obtained on that resolution. • This is not a process of impeachment, nor can the President or the Prime Minister directly remove the Vice- President. Ans. (b) Functioning of Parliament

subject: Polity
question: What is the role of the Speaker in case of a tied vote in the Lok Sabha election?
options: Refers the decision to the President
explanation: Absence of initial voting: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha does not vote in the House under normal circumstances. This ensures their neutrality as the presiding officer of the House. • According to Article 100 of the Indian Constitution, if during voting on a motion the number of votes of the government and the opposition becomes equal, then the Speaker has the right to cast a vote. This vote is called the “casting vote.”

subject: Polity
question: According to the Constitution of India, what is the quorum required to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament?
options: One-third of the total number of members of the House.
Fifty members in the Lok Sabha and twenty-five members in the Rajya Sabha.
One-tenth of the total number of members of the House.
One-fourth of the total number of members of the House.
explanation: Quorum is the minimum number of members whose presence is required before the proceedings of the House can legally commence. • According to Article 100(3) of the Indian Constitution, the quorum for a meeting of either House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) must be one-tenth (1/10th) of the total number of members of the House. • According to Article 100(4), if there is no quorum in the House, it is the duty of the presiding officer (Speaker or Chairman) to either adjourn the House or suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.

subject: Polity
question: What is the basis for the allocation of seats to states in the Lok Sabha?
explanation: Under Article 81 of the Constitution, seats in the Lok Sabha are allocated to states based on population. Currently, this allocation is based on the 1971 Census. The 84th Constitutional Amendment Act (2001) has frozen this allocation until the year 2026.

subject: Polity
question: Who acts as the chairperson during a joint meeting of both houses of Parliament?
explanation: According to Article 118(4) of the Constitution, the Joint Sitting of both Houses of Parliament is always presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. In their absence, the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha takes charge, and if they are also unavailable, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha fulfills this responsibility. • Note - The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice President) never presides over a joint sitting.

subject: Polity
question: Which type of bill cannot originate in the State Legislative Council of an Indian state? I. Money Bill II. Ordinary Bill
explanation: According to Article 198 of the Indian Constitution, the powers of the State Legislative Council are very limited regarding Money Bills. This provision is almost similar to the one between the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha at the Centre regarding a Money Bill. • The Legislative Council has the right to give its recommendations on a Money Bill only within 14 days, but it cannot reject or amend it.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following can recommend the creation of a Legislative Council in an Indian state?
explanation: Under Article 169, if the Legislative Assembly of a State passes a resolution by a majority of its total membership and by a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting, then Parliament can create or abolish the Legislative Council in that State. • Currently, the Legislative Council exists in only 6 States of India (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana).

subject: Polity
question: A Bill passed by the Indian State Legislature is sent to the Governor under_______.
explanation: Under Article 200, when a bill is passed by the State Legislature, it is presented to the Governor for his assent. In this situation, the Governor has four options— he may give his assent to the bill, withhold his assent, return the bill for reconsideration (if it is not a Money Bill), or reserve the bill for the consideration of the President.

subject: Polity
question: In the context of the Indian Parliament, the________ Reading refers to the discussion on the motion that the Bill or the Bill, as amended, be passed.
explanation: In the process of passing any bill, there are three readings. During the third reading, the discussion is limited to whether the bill should be accepted or rejected as a whole; no detailed amendments are made at this stage. If the majority of the house supports it, the bill is considered passed.

subject: Polity
question: What is the first hour of Lok Sabha proceedings called?
explanation: The first hour of a sitting in both Houses of Parliament is called ‘Question Hour’, in which members ask questions to ministers regarding the government’s works and policies. • The time immediately following the Question Hour is called ‘Zero Hour’, where members can raise important issues without prior notice.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following qualifications is required to contest the election of the President of India? I. He or she must hold any office of profit under Central government. II. He or she must qualify to become member of House of the People.
explanation: A candidate for the office of President must possess the qualifications to become a member of the Lok Sabha and should not hold any office of profit (Article 58). For the Vice-President, eligibility for the Rajya Sabha is necessary, whereas for the President, it is for the Lok Sabha.

subject: Polity
question: President shall from time to time summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but months shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.
explanation: Under Article 85 of the Indian Constitution, the President is empowered to summon (call) the sessions of Parliament. It is mandatory to ensure that there is no long gap in the proceedings of Parliament, so that the accountability of the government is maintained. • The gap between two sessions of Parliament cannot be more than 6 months.

subject: Polity
question: For how long a person can serve as a minister without being a member of either House of Parliament of India?
explanation: According to Article 75(5), any person can remain a minister for a maximum period of 6 months without being a Member of Parliament (MP). Before the expiry of this period, it is mandatory for the person to be elected as a member of either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha.

subject: Polity
question: Rajya Sabha is required to return a Money Bill passed and transmitted by Lok Sabha within a period of______ days from the date of its receipt.
explanation: In the Indian Constitution, the Lok Sabha has been given more powers in the case of a Money Bill, while the role of the Rajya Sabha is limited and merely advisory. According to Article 109, the Rajya Sabha can delay a Money Bill for only 14 days. If it does not return the bill with or without suggestions within this period, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses.

subject: Polity
question: Which of the following bill provides details on the imposition, abolition, or regulation of taxes proposed in the budget?
explanation: Under Article 110 of the Indian Constitution, the ‘Finance Bill’ provides details regarding the imposition of new taxes, the abolition of old taxes, or the amendment of the existing tax structure proposed in the budget. It is presented annually with the budget so that the financial policies of the government can receive legal recognition.

subject: Polity
question: Who decides whether a bill is a Money Bill or not?
options: Speaker of the House of the People
explanation: In the Indian Constitution, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha has special powers regarding a Money Bill. According to Article 110 (3), if any question arises whether a bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha shall be final.

subject: Polity
question: The Parliament of India can legislate on a state subject if_____.
options: Council of state passes a resolution by 2/3 majority of the members present
Lok Sabha passes a resolution by simple majority
Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by simple majority
explanation: Under Article 249, if the Rajya Sabha declares that in the national interest, Parliament should make a law on a subject in the State List, and this resolution is passed by a 2/3 majority of the members present and voting, then Parliament can make a law on that State subject.

subject: Polity
question: What is the minimum age to become a member of Rajya Sabha?
explanation: Under Article 84(b) of the Indian Constitution, the minimum age for members of Parliament has been fixed at 30 years to become a member of the Rajya Sabha and 25 years to become a member of the Lok Sabha.

subject: Polity
question: Who can dissolve the House of the People of India before its term ends?
options: Speaker of the House of the People
explanation: According to Article 85(2) (b) of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha. The President exercises this power on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers. • The Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Chief Justice, or the Election Commission does not have this authority.

subject: Polity
question: The practice in the Parliament where the demands for grants are put to a vote after the passage of the time limit for discussion is called_________.
explanation: In the Indian Parliament, Guillotine is a parliamentary procedure whereby the remaining demands for grants are put to vote without discussion after the time allotted for discussion on the demands for grants ends. Its objective is to complete financial business on time. • A motion is a general proposal made in the House on any subject, a cut motion is a proposal to reduce the amount of a demand for grant, whereas a point of order refers to an objection raised against the proceedings of the House regarding a breach of procedure or rules.

subject: Polity
question: Under which Article can the President promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is not in session, and how long do these last?
options: Article 123; until Parliament reconvenes or 6 weeks thereafter
Article 213; until next session of state legislature
explanation: Under Article 123, the President can promulgate an ordinance when Parliament is not in session. • This ordinance remains valid for 6 weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, unless it is approved or repealed earlier. • Article 213: This relates to the promulgation of an ordinance by the Governor.

subject: Polity
question: Fill in the blanks: A Bill that “imposes a new tax” is categorised at the Centre as a ___ Bill.
explanation: A bill that imposes a new tax is classified as a Money Bill in the Centre. Bills related to the subjects of Article 110 of the Indian Constitution (taxation, revenue, borrowing, expenditure, etc.) fall under the category of Money Bill. • Ordinary Bill: It relates to ordinary laws, not the imposition of taxes. • Private Member’s Bill: It is introduced by any private member (other than a Minister). • Constitutional Amendment Bill: It relates to the amendment of the Constitution.

subject: Polity
question: Which authority decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill?
explanation: According to Article 110(3), the decision of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha on whether a bill is a Money Bill or not is final. • It relates only to the subjects mentioned in Article 110 (taxation, Consolidated Fund, public expenditure, etc.). • A Financial Bill may include other financial matters along with the provisions of a Money Bill. Ans. (c) 55. Consider the following statements:

subject: Polity
question: How are Money Bills handled in both Houses of Parliament and State Legislatures with bicameralism under the Constitution?
options: Rajya Sabha must approve Money Bills within 14 days
In States, the Legislative Council can amend a Money Bill within 14 days
Both Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils have equal powers on Money Bills
Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils can only make recommendations within 14 days
explanation: According to the constitutional provisions (Articles 110-109 and 199- 198), the Upper House, Rajya Sabha/ Legislative Council, can withhold a Money Bill for only 14 days and can only make recommendations, which the Lok Sabha/Legislative Assembly is not bound to accept. • In the case of Money Bills, the approval of the Rajya Sabha is not mandatory, the amendments of the Legislative Council are not binding, and the Lower House (Lok Sabha/ Legislative Assembly) holds the primary authority. • The final decision on whether a bill is a Money Bill is made by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha/Speaker of the Legislative Assembly.

subject: Polity
question: Fill in the blanks: The Parliament can create a new All- India Service by a resolution in the ___.
explanation: • Following a resolution by the Rajya Sabha, the Parliament creates a new All India Service by enacting a law. A resolution to this effect must be passed by the Rajya Sabha with at least a 2/3rd majority of the members present and voting. • There is a provision for the creation of a new All India Service under Article 312.

subject: Polity
question: Arrange the following steps in the correct legislative process for the passage of a Money Bill in India: A) Introduction of money bill in Lok Sabha B) Passage in Lok Sabha C) Transmission to Rajya Sabha D) Presentation of President’s assent
explanation: • A Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha. • It is mandatory for it to be passed by the Lok Sabha. • It is sent to the Rajya Sabha; which can only make recommendations (within 14 days). • Finally, the bill is presented to the President for assent. • The final decision on whether a bill is a Money Bill or not lies with the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, which cannot be challenged in any court.

subject: Polity
question: The members of Rajya Sabha are elected for a term of______.
explanation: • Rajya Sabha is a permanent house which is never dissolved, but the tenure of its members is 6 years. • Every two years, one-third (1/3) of its members retire, ensuring the continuity of the house.

subject: Polity
question: Consider the below statements: 1. The Governor is the state’s constitutional head. 2. He acts solely on Council’s advice. Which of the above statements holds true regarding the Governor’s executive powers?
explanation: According to Articles 153 and 154, the Governor is the constitutional head of the State. All executive powers of the State are vested in the Governor. • Article 163(1) makes it clear that the Governor should act on the advice of the Council of Ministers, except in those matters where they are required to act in their own discretion.

subject: Polity
question: Which discretionary power allows a Governor to reserve a bill passed by the state legislature for the consideration of the President?
options: To send a report to the President for the imposition of President’s Rule.
To reserve a bill for the President’s consideration.
To grant pardon in certain cases.
To summon, prorogue, and dissolve the state legislative assembly.
explanation: Under Article 200 of the Indian Constitution, the Governor has special discretionary powers. • When a bill passed by the State Legislature is sent to the Governor for assent, the Governor has four options: to give assent, to withhold assent, to return the bill for reconsideration (if it is not a Money Bill), and to reserve the bill for the consideration of the President.

subject: Polity
question: Which article provides for the appointment of Governors in India?
explanation: In the Indian Constitution, Article 155 provides that the Governor of a state shall be appointed by the President of India through a warrant under his hand and seal.
